sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose and list of models
sections.what: Describes the benchmark: test several open-source models on finance-style tasks, then pick the best. The docstring lists five tasks and four models.
sections.why: The docstring explains the intent; the code tests fewer models and tasks than it describes.
sections.watch_out: The docstring lists four models and five tasks, but the code tests three models and two tasks, so the description is out of date.

sections.name: ModelBenchmark (part 1)
sections.title: Summary test and class setup
sections.what: Holds the model list and a test that asks a model to summarise a short earnings paragraph into three bullet points. It counts a pass if the answer contains a bullet or numbered item, and records response speed.
sections.why: Likely reason: a quick automatic check gives a pass or fail for each model.
sections.watch_out: The pass check is loose, so any hyphen anywhere in the answer counts as a bullet and a poor summary can still pass.

sections.name: ModelBenchmark: test_formula_explanation
sections.title: Formula explanation test
sections.what: Asks a model to explain an Excel NPV formula and checks whether the answer mentions net present value. Records response time and words per second.
sections.why: Likely reason: tests a finance-specific skill the app's explanation features depend on.
sections.watch_out: Words per second is a rough speed measure, not a true token rate.

sections.name: ModelBenchmark: _select_best_models
sections.title: Choosing the fastest passing model
sections.what: Runs both tests on each model, averages their times, and keeps models with no errors. Then it picks the lowest average time and assigns that model to every agent type. If no model is kept, it uses a fixed default set.
sections.why: Likely reason: speed is the only ranking used, which suits an app that must respond quickly.
sections.watch_out: A call that fails returns zero seconds rather than an error, so a model that is not running can be picked as fastest.

sections.name: main
sections.title: Runs the benchmark and prints results
sections.what: Runs the full benchmark, prints the chosen model for each agent type as formatted text, and returns the same result. A comment notes that saving to a config file is an idea, not something done.
sections.why: Lets someone run the benchmark from the command line and read the answer.
sections.watch_out: The json module is only imported when the file runs directly, so importing main from another file would fail.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Starts benchmark when run directly
sections.what: When the file runs from the command line, it imports json and calls the main function. Importing the file from elsewhere does not start any tests.
sections.why: Likely reason: prevents the slow benchmark from starting by accident when another file loads this one.
sections.watch_out: Running it makes real calls to every listed model, so Ollama must be running with the models downloaded.

summary: Test script that tries a few open-source AI models on sample finance tasks and picks the fastest one that does not error.
purpose: Helps choose which local model each agent should use.
why: Likely reason: model speed and quality differ between computers and models, so the app measures them rather than guessing.
how: Runs each model in the model list through a summary test and a formula explanation test, averages their response times, and keeps models with no errors. It then chooses the fastest and assigns it to every agent type.
inputs: The model names listed in the class, and a running Ollama server reached through the base agent.
outputs: A dictionary mapping each agent type to one model name. When run from the command line, it prints this dictionary.
risks: A failed model call returns zero time, so a model that is not working can look like the fastest. The quality check is loose, and the choice ignores it.
debug: If the chosen model seems wrong, look at the per-model results for zero latency. Confirm Ollama is running and each model has been downloaded. Note that the docstring lists four models and five tasks, but the code tests three models and two tasks.
